title: Eight new paintings for the second cut of Until We Return
provenance: Each shot was commissioned as an individual full-frame painting using the original text prompt stored with its record. The artists’ visual brief was informed by existing game and film paintings. No external painting, scan or photograph was submitted to the generator.
acquisition: Original 1672 × 941 RGB PNG images, center-fitted to 1600 × 900 with Pillow Lanczos and encoded as RGB WebP at quality 92, method 6. Coordinates are fractions of the released frame measured from its upper left. Each output was decoded and visually reviewed. A preliminary auger composition was replaced before the final edit.

paintings.composition: Three men carry a round spar up to a forked upright at the edge of the new house.
paintings.evidence_and_staging: S001, chapter II, pp. 15–16, records the use of salvaged spars. The raising gesture, three workers and choice of joint are staged. Their names are unspecified.

Restrained, uncontrived composition with a precise center of interest. Intelligible on a small screen, enough tonal and color range; never overwhelmingly murky. Hands and tools have correct anatomy and mechanics. Compose for a 16:9 frame with objects retained inside a modest 7% outer safety margin. An exterior daytime action seen from shoulder height at Carnley Harbour in a break in the weather, the framing of a rough house beside native trees. Strong diagonals; a worn light-colored salvaged round spar is being passed up into a fork in a new upright. Three mariners actually share the weight, carrying the spar at different points: nearer man in faded blue wool in lower left seen from back, taller man in oatmeal shirt (sleeves up) at middle, third partly obscured behind near the upright at right steadying it. Their hands are directly in contact with its underside, footwork and weight credible. Sail ties, one improvised timber trestle, plain wood. The beam must enter from the middle of the frame, not through a face. It is one small single-storey wreck-survivor hut, no preexisting building, no heavy modern machinery, no mass of loose scaffolding. In straw grass behind them are sparse southern rātā, a horizontal glimpse of a cold grey inlet and distant worn headland. Thick pale limber timber cutting across dark blue foliage, restrained warm sunlight on sleeves. A deliberate story moment of the heavy beam entering its notch; not a group portrait.

paintings.composition: A thumb and forefinger lift a little pale pawn above red and white figures cut from slats.
paintings.evidence_and_staging: S004, p. 160, records a soot-and-lime board, red and white chessmen and a pocketknife. Board position, window and pawns’ silhouettes are staging.

paintings.composition: A hand sets a wedge against a rectangular ballast bar supported by timber.
paintings.evidence_and_staging: S001, chapter VII, pp. 79–80, records using iron ballast as an anvil. S004, chapter XVIII, describes a flat four-sided bar roughly fourteen inches long in a timber frame. The wedge and gesture are staging.

Close detailed three-quarter view inside a makeshift sea-worn shed near the survivors’ hut; daylight comes down onto a roughly fourteen-inch-long, square-section salvaged dark iron ship-ballast bar, 14 × 3½ × 3½ inches in life, smooth four-sided straight RECTANGULAR bar horizontal, plain flat ends, neither an anvil horn nor modern blacksmith anvil. paintings.composition: Two hands work a skin-and-timber bellows whose tapering nozzle reaches the charcoal.
paintings.evidence_and_staging: S004, chapter XVIII, describes the sealskin joints and covering, three wooden panels, copper tube, masonry and bricks, and a salvaged copper-sheet roof. Hand placement and the view through the shed are staged.

paintings.composition: The iron end of an improvised hand auger rests on a thick timber beside a shallow unfinished recess and pale shavings.
paintings.evidence_and_staging: S001, chapter VII, pp. 81–83, records the failure to make an auger suitable for the heavy frames. The spoon-shaped tip, trial piece and shallow recess illustrate that problem. The precise design of the failed tool is unrecorded here.
paintings.prompt: Compose a single fine-art oil painting in 16:9 widescreen as a close insert in a historical ship-carpenter’s film. A windowless corner of a timber shed in 1865. EXACTLY the tactile workbench still life visible within the composition: one worn improvised hand auger with a dark wrought-iron spoon-shaped end and a simple wooden crossbar handle, lying diagonally on a big rough beam beside its unfinished shallow circular recess and a few fresh shavings. Backdrop is exclusively the dark weathered timber wall inside the shed, gently out of focus. Frame so tightly that there is no source of light visible, only indirect daylight falling across the objects from off-camera left. No outdoors is visible through any part of the room. The iron and fresh shavings are the visual focus. Work in similar dark indigo-ochre muted tones to a serious naturalist maritime oil painting, fine tactile brush marks, weathered surfaces, no bright filter. Side lighting on the dulled silvery end. Horizontal composition set at the carpenter's eye level, elegant stillness, no signage, no hands, no people, no lettering, no framing border.

paintings.composition: A plank is held fair along the dinghy’s older sheer while a second worker seats a fastening.
paintings.evidence_and_staging: S001, chapters VII–VIII, describes raising and trying the old dinghy. The camera angle, tools in these men’s hands, and the first fastening chosen are reconstructions.

Looking lengthwise along the curved sheer of the Grafton’s little wooden ship's dinghy beached upright in a rough timber cradle at Carnley Harbour, before the ocean attempt in 1865. Paint a tactile MEDIUM-CLOSE shot at boat-builder’s eye height. Two sailors’ hands work together: one weather-beaten hand stretches the long new lighter side plank flush along the existing upper strake, the other worker's small plain wooden mallet angled to seat a fastening or light spacer. The board is visibly being added ON TOP of the older dark side to raise freeboard, continuous and properly following the hull curve. Lower body of hull and its parallel overlapping strakes at bottom, old grey oar resting inside, thin band of sea and scrub shore softly glimpsed at top left. Hands and wrists arise from opposite sides, sleeves worn navy and oatmeal, no floating arms. A little warm side light on the pale plank after rain; intimate material study with evidence of the original hull. No full ship scale, propeller, power tools, nontechnical ropes crossed across the work or modern screws.

paintings.composition: A donor and a civilian at a shop counter take the weight of a folded wool blanket between them. The doorway opens onto wet streets.
paintings.evidence_and_staging: S001, chapter IX, pp. 98–99, records Invercargill residents contributing clothes and blankets for the two remaining men. The donor, clerk, shop, garment colours and handoff are anonymous staging.

Middle-ground action, a civilian wool-clad woman at left places a folded scrap-edged blue-grey wool blanket from her arms into the waiting hands of a clerk or merchant in a simple brown waistcoat and rolled shirt sleeves to the right of the counter. paintings.evidence_and_staging: S001, chapter XI, pp. 117–118, records the meal of fish and potatoes aboard Flying Scud. Service, lighting, crockery, cabin and poses are reconstructed.

Very intimate, warm eveningside view at table height on the small rescue cutter Flying Scud moored in Camp Cove in August 1865. A small worn shipboard deal table near the hull’s ribs. At left a seaman's hand in a worn grey-blue coat draws a warm plate of cooked fish and potatoes toward him; a second hand at far right quietly sets a fresh mug near the plate farther away.
